_what_this_is: Tier-G Ingredient KB entry for Centella asiatica / madecassoside / asiaticoside ('cica') — built to the ADR-002 quality bar and the genistein gold-standard shape (v2-lite + additive Tier-G fields). Adversarially reviewed: every citation URL verified to resolve before inclusion.

ingredient.what_it_is: A creeping herb native to tropical Southeast and South Asia, used for centuries in Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine. Its four key triterpenoid saponins — madecassoside, asiaticoside, madecassic acid, and asiatic acid — work across complementary pathways: supporting procollagen synthesis, quenching free radicals, and helping skin look visibly calmer and more comfortable. The 'cica' name in K-beauty derives from the French word cicatrisation (scar formation), but in a cosmetic context the relevant story is appearance support and barrier comfort, not medical wound repair.

marketing_vs_reality.reality: The wound-healing and scar-repair research behind 'cica' is largely pharmaceutical-grade clinical work. A leave-on cosmetic formulation operates at far lower concentrations and without occlusion — what it can honestly deliver is supporting the skin's barrier appearance, helping skin look calmer and less reactive, and supplying antioxidant support. 'Heals wounds' is a drug claim; cosmetic-safe language is 'supports the look of a stronger barrier' and 'skin appears calmer'.

Triterpenoids modulate inflammatory cytokine pathways in cell and animal models, but a cosmetic product cannot make anti-inflammatory drug claims. The honest cosmetic translation: madecassoside and asiaticoside help skin look less red and irritated after exposure to stressors — a look/feel outcome, not a treatment outcome.

overview: Centella asiatica's triterpenoids support procollagen synthesis via TGF-β/Smad signaling, scavenge free radicals, enhance barrier-related proteins (filaggrin, involucrin), and help skin look calmer. Best evidence is at grade B — strong mechanism + some human fibroblast and in-vivo data, but large-scale RCT evidence in cosmetic formulations is limited. Traditional-use heritage spans millenia; K-beauty catapulted it to mainstream global status in the 2010s.

benefits.what_it_means: Skin looks and feels more comfortable; helps maintain surface hydration and reduce the appearance of redness after stressors like environmental exposure or new product introduction.
benefits.mechanism: Madecassoside upregulates filaggrin and involucrin (structural proteins in the stratum corneum) and enhances skin hydration in vitro and in vivo; extract saponins normalize skin-surface pH toward a healthy acid mantle (~pH 5), supporting barrier integrity.

benefits.what_it_means: Over weeks of use, skin may look firmer and more luminous. Not a retinoid-speed result — a gradual procollagen support story.
benefits.mechanism: Asiaticoside activates type-I procollagen synthesis via TGF-β receptor kinase-independent Smad signaling in dermal fibroblasts. Madecassoside additionally stimulates type-III collagen. In cultured human fibroblasts, both compounds increased type-I collagen secretion by ~25–30%; madecassoside was the only compound to also significantly boost type-III collagen.

benefits.what_it_means: Supportive daily antioxidant; helps skin look less fatigued after UV or pollution exposure. Combines well with vitamin C or niacinamide for a multi-target approach.
benefits.mechanism: Centella extract scavenges DPPH free radicals with ~83% inhibition at 1 mg/mL — comparable to grape seed extract and just below vitamin C (88%). Phenolic and flavonoid constituents drive the antioxidant capacity via redox-reduction. Madecassoside also activates autophagy to reduce overall oxidative damage in skin cells.

benefits.what_it_means: Skin looks less reactive, less red, and more even-toned — particularly valued after exfoliation routines, retinoid use, or environmental stress.
benefits.mechanism: Triterpene saponins reduce prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) synthesis and suppress pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β) in cell models. The cosmetic appearance outcome is visibly calmer, more even-looking skin — not a treatment of an inflammatory condition.

watchouts.what_to_do: Well-tolerated in the vast majority of users, but sensitization to Centella asiatica has been reported in a small number of individuals. Patch-test on new-to-skin barrier-disrupted or eczema-prone skin.

Isolated asiaticoside at high pharmaceutical concentrations has shown mild phototoxic potential in some studies. Cosmetic concentrations are significantly lower; no actionable photosensitivity concern for typical leave-on products, but daytime SPF use is best practice.

consider_separating: high-concentration exfoliating acids (AHA/BHA) in same step — use cica as the calming follow-up step, not mixed into the acid
notes: Particularly effective as a buffer layer after actives (retinoids, acids) to support the look of a calmer barrier.
Traditional K-beauty 'cica' positioning: post-procedure and reactive-skin first aid — this is where the performance profile is clearest.
Gradual collagen-support story — evaluate at 8–12 weeks.
AM and PM appropriate; no interactions with SPF.

evidence.summary: Strong peer-reviewed mechanistic evidence (TGF-β/Smad collagen pathway, antioxidant DPPH benchmarks, filaggrin/involucrin upregulation) plus human fibroblast in-vitro data and some in-vivo animal data. No large-scale placebo-controlled RCTs specifically in cosmetic formulations at typical use concentrations — hence B not A. Traditional use heritage across Ayurvedic, TCM, and French wound-care traditions is centuries-old and convergent with the mechanistic picture, reinforcing the confidence.
